analysis.one_liner: Ends giveaway of federal oil shale land, forcing old mining claims into royalty-paying leases or abandonment.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in March 1990, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended a leftover of the 1872 Mining Law: corporations holding oil shale claims located before 1920 could claim full private title to federal land for almost nothing. Instead, claim holders would have had to choose within 180 days — convert the claim to a 20-year federal lease paying at least a 12.5% royalty, or keep the claim only by doing $1,000 of work on it every year and filing annual affidavits; doing neither would count as abandoning the claim. It also barred companies holding old claims from getting new federal oil shale leases on top, and required reclamation bonds before any ground was disturbed. The bill cleared the Senate Energy Committee and sat on the Senate calendar for nine months, but no vote was ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would collect at least a 12.5% royalty on any oil shale removed from public land instead of losing title to it for 1872-law prices, and the public at large, which keeps the land in federal ownership with bond-backed reclamation guarantees.

how_it_helps.text: Blocks new patents — full private ownership deeds — for pre-1920 oil shale mining claims after January 25, 1989, except for applications where every patent requirement had already been fully met by that date.

Forces holders of old claims to choose within 180 days: convert to a 20-year federal lease paying at least a 12.5% royalty, or keep the claim only by performing $1,000 of annual work and filing yearly affidavits with the Bureau of Land Management — failure on either path is treated as abandonment of the claim.

Prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing a federal oil shale lease to any company that controls, or is controlled by, an entity still holding an 1872-era mining claim, preventing one company from holding claims and leases at once.

Requires anyone holding a claim or lease under the bill to reclaim the site and post a bond guaranteeing reclamation before the land is disturbed, and applies the same reclamation and bonding rules to new Mineral Leasing Act leases.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations holding oil shale mining claims located before the 1920 Mineral Leasing Act: they would lose the path to cheap full-title patents, pay a 12.5% royalty if they leased, spend $1,000 per claim per year to hold claims otherwise, post reclamation bonds, and lose claims outright for missing any deadline.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies holding old oil shale claims

drawbacks.text: Companies that located claims decades before 1920 relied on the 1872 law's promise of eventual patents; the bill's forced election with automatic abandonment effectively extinguishes those long-held property expectations on the government's terms.

The keep-the-claim option is cheap: $1,000 of annual work per claim lets holders retain vast oil shale acreage indefinitely for a nominal sum while waiting for the resource to become economic, so the bill does little to unblock the land.

The committee substitute was softer than the bill as introduced — the original flatly banned all new patents after January 25, 1989, while the reported version set out circumstances under which pending patent applications could still receive full or limited patents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For taxpayers the trade is lopsided in the public's favor: land worth far more than 1872-law patent prices stays public or produces a 12.5% royalty, and reclamation gets bonded up front. The real costs fall on a small set of claim-holding companies, and the strongest good-faith objection is reliance on century-old law; a fairer bill might have offered compensation. The bill's biggest design weakness runs the other way — the $1,000-a-year claim-holding option is cheap enough that companies could lock up the land for a century at trivial cost.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy Committee approved it and put it on the Senate calendar in March 1990, but no one ever brought it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Wirth introduced the bill on January 25, 1989 with Senators Johnston and Bumpers, and it was read twice and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The Subcommittee on Mineral Resources Development held hearings on July 31, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-248.

On March 8, 1990 the full committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on March 29, 1990 Senator Johnston reported it to the Senate with a written report and additional views filed.

The original version flatly barred new patents and gave claim holders 180 days to elect a lease or comply with new annual work requirements; the reported substitute instead required notice to claim holders, allowed some pending patent applications to receive full or limited patents, and kept the abandonment deadline and reclamation bonding.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 494) on March 29, 1990, and no further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding pre-1920 oil shale mining claims are better off because the bill died: they kept their claims and the possibility of full-title patents rather than facing a 180-day election, royalties, annual work requirements, and bond-backed reclamation. Taxpayers never gained the royalty stream or the reclamation guarantees.

industries.industry: Oil shale mining claim holders (companies with pre-1920 claims)
industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to convert federal oil shale land into full private title for nominal patent fees, and would instead face a 12.5% royalty, annual work and filing requirements, reclamation bonds, and automatic claim abandonment for missing deadlines. Their gain if the bill died was keeping claims worth billions in federal oil shale at essentially no cost.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining under the 1872 Mining Law
industries.note: The bill carved oil shale out of the 1872 law's claim-and-patent system, and its structure — royalties, annual requirements, abandonment for noncompliance — pointed toward tighter terms for patent-era claims generally. The broader hardrock industry's interest ran against that precedent.
